cards.title: Core idea
cards.body: Every Kubernetes API request follows one fixed pipeline in kube-apiserver: authentication, authorization (usually RBAC), mutating admission, schema validation, validating admission, then save to etcd. It is the single front door for humans, CI pipelines, controllers and kubelets.

cards.title: How it works
cards.body: Admission runs only on writes. Kubernetes has no User object; a normal user is just a name taken from a credential issued by an external system like a certificate authority or identity provider. The most common RBAC mistake is using the cluster-wide pair when a namespaced Role and RoleBinding would do.

questions.q: Does Kubernetes store users and passwords?
questions.a: No. There is no User resource. The user name comes from the credential, such as a certificate CN or OIDC claim.

questions.q: What order do mutating and validating admission run in?
questions.a: Mutating admission, then schema validation, then validating admission.

questions.q: What is the most common RBAC mistake?
questions.a: Using ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding when a namespaced Role and RoleBinding would be enough.
